text: A and I both want the trailer in the next few weeks, and neither of us is backing down. B's pad is where it lives, so she is stuck in the middle. Can you help the three of us sort this out?

Thanks for bringing me in, C. I'm glad to help the three of you sort this out. My plan is to collect each person's needs and concerns on one list, then test any proposal against that list in the open.

Before we talk about who gets the trailer when, I want to hear from everyone. So, what do you need? Please tell me: when and how often you want the trailer over the next few weeks, what you want to use it for, what you can contribute to storage, upkeep, and cost, and what would make a shared schedule feel fair to you.

I'll also name my own concerns, and you can push back on any of them. First, I don't want B to end up carrying a fight between you and A, since the trailer sits on her pad. Second, I can't make legal decisions or move money, so whatever we agree has to come from the three of you. Third, I want clear ground rules for scheduling, storage, upkeep, and splitting costs. Fourth, I want to be easy to disagree with, so say so if my list misstates your position. Please keep your answer short and plain, and I'll do the same.

I need the trailer in the next few weeks to haul materials for my home project. Exact days and frequency aren’t set, but I won’t just wait until A is done—I need a turn soon. I can discuss storage, upkeep, and costs, but no amounts or shares are decided. A fair schedule gives each of us clear turns and doesn’t let anyone monopolize it. And yes, B shouldn’t have to mediate between us.

Hello A, C asked me to help the three of you work out a plan for the cargo trailer you bought together. I want to gather each person's needs on one list, then check any proposal against it in the open.

Starting with you: when and how often do you want the trailer over the next few weeks, what do you need it for, what can you put toward storage, upkeep, and cost, and what would make a shared schedule feel fair to you?

I'll name my own concerns too. I don't want B to be stuck in the middle of a disagreement between you and C, since the trailer lives on her pad. I can't make legal decisions or move money, so the plan has to come from the three of you. I want clear ground rules for scheduling, storage, upkeep, and costs. And I want you to tell me when my list gets your position wrong. Short and plain answers are fine.

I want the trailer for weekend trips over the next few weeks; I don’t have exact dates or a set frequency yet. I need flexibility to plan my trips. I’m willing to discuss a fair share of storage, upkeep, and costs, but no amounts are settled. A fair schedule gives each of us a real chance to use it, with dates agreed in advance and room to adjust. Your list sounds right; just don’t assume B has to mediate between C and me.

Hello B, C asked me to help the three of you work out a plan for the cargo trailer you bought together. My approach is to put each person's needs and concerns on one list, then check any proposal against that list in the open.

I especially want to hear from you, because the trailer sits on your pad. What do you need? How much room and access can you live with, what are your limits on people coming and going, what can you put toward storage, upkeep, and cost, and what would make this feel fair to you?

My own concerns, and please disagree if you see them differently: I don't want you to be the one absorbing a disagreement between A and C. I can't make legal decisions or move money, so the plan has to come from the three of you. I want clear rules for scheduling, storage, upkeep, and costs. And I want to be easy to correct, so tell me if I get your position wrong. Short and plain answers are fine.

I’d rather the trailer wasn’t on my pad—it’s in my way, though I agreed to the arrangement when we bought it and feel a bit bad asking. For now, please check with me before coming by. I can’t say what space or money I can offer; the costs and shares aren’t settled, and I rent, so I’d need my landlord’s approval for any change. I haven’t asked him. A fair plan shouldn’t leave me carrying the burden just because it’s on my pad.

Thank you, B. That's useful and it changes the picture, so I'll put it first in the summary: the trailer sits on a rented pad and any change needs your landlord's approval, which you have not asked for. Nobody should push you on that, and you shouldn't feel bad for raising it. I'm adding your points to the list: the trailer is in your way, you want to be asked before people come by, space and money shares aren't settled, and a fair plan must not leave you carrying the burden just because the trailer is on your pad. I've noted that you feel a bit bad asking. That belongs on the list too, because it's a real cost to you. I'm still waiting on A. Once I have A's answer I'll send all three of you one list and invite corrections.
That sounds about right, thanks. I do feel awkward asking, but I’d rather the trailer not stay on my pad indefinitely.

Thanks, C. I'm putting your points on the list: you need the trailer within the next few weeks for a home project, exact days and frequency are open, you want a turn soon rather than after A is done, storage and upkeep and costs are open to discussion with no amounts or shares set, a fair schedule gives each of you clear turns, and it doesn't let anyone monopolize the trailer. You also agree B shouldn't have to mediate. B has replied too. Her news matters for all of us: the pad is rented, so any change in how the trailer is stored there needs her landlord's approval, and she has not asked him yet. She also wants a say before people come by. I'll send the full list to all three of you once A answers, and I'll ask you then to correct anything I've misstated.
Got it. No changes to the pad without the landlord’s approval, and I’ll check with B before coming by. I still need a turn soon, so please keep that on the list.

All three of us have now answered, so here is the list. Please correct anything I have wrong.

One, the trailer belongs to the three of you. Decisions come from you, not from me, and I cannot make legal decisions or move money.

Two, A needs the trailer for weekend trips in the next few weeks. Dates and frequency are not fixed, and A wants room to plan.

Three, C needs it within the next few weeks for a home project. Exact days are not fixed, and C will not wait until A is finished.

Four, B would rather the trailer was not on her pad and feels awkward saying so, though she agreed to the arrangement at purchase.

Five, the pad is rented, so any change there needs B's landlord's approval, which she has not asked for.

Six, B wants to be checked with before anyone comes by.

Seven, storage, upkeep, and cost shares are unsettled. Nobody has named an amount or a share.

Eight, all three of you want clear turns, agreed in advance, with room to adjust and no one monopolizing the trailer.

Nine, all three of you agree B should not have to mediate between A and C.

My own concerns, which you should feel free to argue with. First, if A and C both want the trailer in the next few weeks without dates, an unbooked wish becomes a race, and the person with the loudest claim wins. Booked dates with a notice period fix that. Second, B's "for now" needs a review date, or the trailer drifts on her pad indefinitely. Third, unsettled shares are the most likely thing to break the plan later.

So here is a first proposal. Set up one shared calendar and book days at least a few days ahead. A takes weekend blocks. C takes the days the project needs. B is asked before every pickup and drop-off and can say no to a time. Agree a cost and upkeep split now, even a rough one. Set a review date to decide whether the trailer stays on B's pad and whether she asks her landlord. C, a question that may unlock all of this: can your project work on weekdays, which would leave weekends to A?
I’m not sure yet whether weekdays will work. I can check, but I can’t commit to leaving weekends to A; I still need a turn soon. Let’s put actual dates on the calendar.

Weekdays for C work if that suits the project. I’ll accept a reasonable cap on weekends booked ahead, but let’s agree the number together and make sure I can book my upcoming trips.

For you, B, the review date is the part that matters most. Would a set date, say the end of next month, work for you as the point to decide where the trailer lives next?
End of next month seems reasonable for a review, but I can’t agree to a change on the pad without my landlord’s approval. I’d like the trailer moved off my pad if we can work that out.

Good, that moves us forward. You and A have now each said weekdays may work for C's project, so that is no longer a guess on my part. Here is where the list stands on the open items.

A accepts a reasonable cap on weekends booked ahead and wants to agree the number together, and wants to be sure his upcoming trips get booked. You will not commit to giving up weekends before you know your project dates, and you want real dates on the calendar.

So the next step is dates, from both of you. Please send me the actual days you need, with a first choice and a second, for the next few weeks: C, the days your project needs, weekdays if they work and weekends if they must; A, your trip dates. Send them to all three of us so we see the same picture. Once the dates are in front of us, we can set the cap on weekends booked ahead with a number we all pick, and fix a review date at the end of next month.

B's position is now clear too: she would like the trailer moved off her pad, and nothing changes there without her landlord's approval. That is a separate track from the dates. If any of you has a second place to keep it, say so now, and a paid storage option is worth costing out before the review date. I cannot move money or make that call; you three can.
I don’t have my project dates yet, so I can’t give first and second choices today. I’ll check the schedule and send actual dates to all three of you. I don’t have another storage place to suggest.

Thanks, A. That is exactly the kind of flexibility that makes a plan work. C says weekdays may suit the project but cannot commit until he knows his dates. Here is where the list stands.

C will send dates. You will send your trip dates. We set the cap on weekends booked ahead together as a number you all pick, and I will make sure your upcoming trips are booked before the cap takes effect. We fix a review date at the end of next month.

Please send your actual trip days, first choice and second, to all three of us for the next few weeks. Please also send your view of a fair cap on weekends booked ahead, for example two or three weekends in any month. A number on the table is easier to argue with than a principle.

B's position is now clear. She would like the trailer moved off her pad, and nothing changes there without her landlord's approval. If you know a second place to keep it, or want to cost out paid storage, say so. I cannot move money or decide that; you three can.

I don’t have exact trip dates to send yet, so I can’t give real first and second choices. I’ll send them as soon as I’ve pinned them down. My preference is a cap of two weekends per month, with my upcoming trips booked before it applies. I don’t know another place to store it, but I’m open to comparing paid-storage costs.

Thank you, B. The end of next month is now on the list as the review date. I have also recorded your clear point that you would like the trailer moved off your pad, and that nothing changes there without your landlord's approval. That is a goal, not a demand on you to solve it alone.

C says weekdays may suit his project but cannot commit until he knows his dates. A accepts a cap on weekends booked ahead and wants to agree the number together. So the next step is dates from both of them.

For you, B, two questions. Would you be willing to test the idea of a paid storage option, with the cost shared, and would you want your landlord asked at all if the trailer moves off your pad? I cannot move money or make those calls, and you should not have to carry the cost of a change that helps everyone. If you would rather not answer until the dates are in, that is fine; say so and I will come back to it.
I’m willing to look at a shared paid-storage option, but I can’t commit to a cost yet. If the trailer moves off my pad, my landlord would need to approve the change; I haven’t asked him.

Here is where we stand, C, and what is still open.

Settled on the list: the three of you decide and I do not; B wants the trailer off her pad and any change there needs her landlord's approval; B is asked before pickups and drop-offs; the three of you agree cost and upkeep shares; there is a cap on weekends booked ahead, with the number picked together; the review date is the end of next month; and weekdays may work for your project, which you will confirm.

Still open: your project dates and A's trip dates, and the weekend cap number. A has not yet sent trip dates, so please send yours to all three of us when you have them, and I will push A for his in the same round.

On storage, B is willing to look at shared paid storage but cannot commit to a cost, and no one has a second place to suggest. Costing out one paid storage option is worth doing before the review date. I cannot move money or make that call; you three can.

Finally, my concern about B's "for now" has eased now that a review date exists. My concern about unsettled shares has not. Put a rough number on the table soon, even if you revise it.
I don’t have project dates to send yet; I’ll confirm whether weekdays work and send actual choices to all three. I don’t have a cost or upkeep share to propose until we know the costs.
